tldr: The paper introduces ChemToolAgent (CTA), an enhanced chemistry agent with 29 tools, and finds that while tool augmentation substantially improves performance on specialized chemistry tasks, it does not consistently outperform base LLMs on general chemistry questions due to increased reasoning errors from added cognitive load.
contributions: Introducing ChemToolAgent (CTA), an enhanced chemistry agent with 29 tools (16 new, 6 enhanced from ChemCrow) built on the ReAct framework

Conducting a comprehensive evaluation of tool-augmented agents across diverse chemistry tasks, including specialized tasks (SMolInstruct) and general exam-style questions (MMLU-Chemistry, SciBench-Chemistry, GPQA-Chemistry)
Performing manual error analysis with a chemistry expert, revealing that tool errors dominate on specialized tasks (>99%) while reasoning errors account for over 90% on general chemistry questions
methods: The authors developed ChemToolAgent using the ReAct framework with 29 tools categorized into general, molecule, and reaction tools. They evaluated CTA against two baselines: state-of-the-art base LLMs (GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet) and ChemCrow. Datasets included SMolInstruct for specialized chemistry tasks (14 molecule- and reaction-centric tasks) and MMLU-Chemistry, SciBench-Chemistry, and GPQA-Chemistry for general chemistry questions spanning high school, college, and graduate levels. Manual error analysis was conducted by a chemistry expert and two PhD students on failed samples.
results: CTA substantially outperforms ChemCrow on all chemistry tasks. On specialized tasks (SMolInstruct), CTA demonstrates significant improvements over base LLMs, with tool errors accounting for over 99.0% of errors, mostly from neural network-based tools with inherent imperfections. On general chemistry questions (MMLU-Chemistry, SciBench-Chemistry, GPQA-Chemistry), CTA surprisingly underperforms its base LLM counterparts in most cases. On MMLU-Chemistry, reasoning errors constitute over 90.0%, primarily manifesting as nuanced mistakes at intermediate problem-solving stages such as wrong knowledge/logic (75.0%), wrong final answer (6.3%), and information oversight (4.7%).
limitations: Evaluation uses only GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet as backbones, excluding broader LLMs like Llama-3.2 or Qwen2
The datasets may not fully represent the vast array of real-world chemistry problems
Manual error analysis is limited in scale (one chemistry expert plus two PhD students), potentially introducing bias and missing subtle variations in error types
